tldr: Instead of generating training data, the proposed framework 'QWM' uses a learned world model solely for action selection via tree search during test-time and online environment collection, avoiding the accumulation of model prediction errors while dramatically boosting the sample efficiency and success rate of Q-learning.
hero_caption: The overall architecture of QWM. As shown on the left, a shallow search tree is constructed using actions proposed by the policy and future states predicted by the world model, scoring actions by integrating intermediate and leaf node values. As shown on the right, this tree search is used during both online data collection and evaluation to execute the highest-scoring action.
overview:
When applying reinforcement learning (RL) to complex tasks like robot manipulation, the biggest hurdle is sample efficiency—learning with as few trials as possible. World models, which predict environmental dynamics, have long been viewed as a key lever for sample efficiency because they let agents try things out in imagination like a simulator. However, conventional model-based RL has a major pitfall. Directly training a policy or value function inside an imperfect world model causes model-specific prediction biases (errors) to compound inside the learning loop, leading to performance collapse, especially in long-horizon tasks or with high-dimensional image inputs.

To solve this, the authors fundamentally shifted their perspective. What if, instead of using world models to synthesize training data, we build them on top of standard Q-learning and use them solely as a tool for test-time search (inference-time compute) to select actions? The policy and Q-function updates are always grounded in real transition data collected from the actual environment. Only when deciding which action to execute does the agent ask the world model to imagine a few steps ahead to pick the best move.

This proposed framework, QWM (Q-Learning with World Models), was evaluated on challenging robot control benchmarks, Robomimic and LIBERO. Experiments across both state-based and camera-image (pixel) inputs showed that QWM significantly outperforms modern model-based methods like TD-MPC2 and EfficientZero V2, as well as strong model-free Q-learning baselines like EXPO and RLPD, in both sample efficiency and final success rates.
contributions: Established QWM, a framework that avoids compounding model bias at its core by using world models purely for action selection via inference-time tree search, rather than directly optimizing policies or value functions within model rollouts
Designed a node value aggregation mechanism that combines action-value $Q$-functions with predicted step rewards, departing from conventional model-based methods that rely solely on state value $V$
Demonstrated sample-efficiency gains not only on low-dimensional state tasks but also on image-input tasks (LIBERO) using a diffusion transformer video generation model
Revealed that performing tree search during both online collection and evaluation yields a synergistic benefit in both replay buffer quality and action selection accuracy

sections.heading: Why use world models for inference-time search instead of learning?
sections.summary: Sample efficiency in off-policy RL is becoming increasingly critical, as seen in RL fine-tuning of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. World models offer a lever for efficiency, but optimizing policies inside them accumulates prediction errors. This paper proposes QWM, which uses world models as a search mechanism for action selection on top of solid Q-learning grounded in real data.
sections.details:
Off-policy reinforcement learning in robotics—learning efficiently from collected transition data—has made remarkable progress and is increasingly applied to fine-tuning large VLA models on physical robots. However, when operating robots in the real world, fewer trials are always preferable, making further improvements in sample efficiency highly sought after.

This is where world models (environment simulators that predict next-state changes from states and actions) attract attention. Yet traditional model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) suffers from a severe weakness. When policies or value functions are directly optimized within a learned dynamics model, the model's prediction errors degrade the policy. As horizons lengthen or visual complexity rises, this bias compounds rapidly.

The core insight of this work is remarkably simple. Instead of substituting the world model for real-world interactions, why not use it simply to sharpen the action selection of a standard Q-learning agent?

In the proposed method, QWM, the policy proposes multiple candidate actions from the current state, and the world model conducts a tree search by imagining short-term future rollouts. A Q-function is then used to select the highest-value action. Because the policy and Q-function are trained entirely on real transitions from the actual environment, model errors never corrupt the learning loop itself. This allows QWM to avoid compounding model bias while fully enjoying the sample-efficiency benefits of predictive search.

sections.heading: The intersection of model-based RL and test-time scaling
sections.summary: Prior work spans offline data utilization, synthetic data generation, trajectory optimization via dynamics models, and applying world models to VLAs. Test-time scaling (such as Best-of-N) has also gained traction in LLMs. QWM distinguishes itself by using world models strictly for test-time search in Q-learning without embedding them as data generators inside the training loop.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three primary areas:

- RL with Prior Data: Approaches that combine offline data with online interaction to boost sample efficiency. Prior work has focused on balancing exploration and exploitation, replay buffer sampling ratios, or adapting offline RL algorithms to online settings. QWM is orthogonal to these techniques; it leverages prior data to pretrain the world model, meaning it can be paired with virtually any existing RL fine-tuning algorithm.

- Model-based RL: Approaches that generate synthetic data within world models to augment training (such as Dyna or MBPO), methods that directly optimize policies via model gradients (such as Dreamer), or planners using trajectory optimizers like MPPI or CEM (such as TD-MPC). However, these methods rely heavily on model predictions to construct learning targets, causing bias to compound over long horizons or with high-dimensional images. AlphaZero-style methods using MCTS (Monte Carlo Tree Search) also tend to rely on discrete actions or known simulators. QWM circumvents these issues by restricting the model to test-time action selection while grounding learning in real data.

- Test-Time Scaling and Best-of-$N$ Inference: Test-time scaling—generating and scoring multiple candidates during inference—has shown great success in LLMs and diffusion models. In RL, methods like IDQL sample multiple actions from a policy and pick the best one using a Q-function, but they only evaluate a single step ahead. QWM uses a world model to look ahead and see what happens after an action is taken, enabling significantly higher-quality action evaluation.

sections.heading: Background: Off-policy Q-learning foundations and baselines
sections.summary: This work considers a standard Markov Decision Process (MDP), pretraining a world model on offline data before proceeding with online RL. As foundations for QWM, two representative state-of-the-art Q-learning methods are adopted: EXPO, which pairs a base policy with a lightweight editing policy, and RLPD, which uses a high UTD ratio and ensemble critics.
sections.details:
We consider an MDP defined by state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, initial state distribution $\rho$, reward function $r$, discount factor $\gamma$, and transition dynamics $T(s'|s,a)$. The goal is to find a policy $\pi$ that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted reward.

In this work, a world model $M_\psi(s'|s,a)$ that predicts the next state from the current state and action is pretrained on a previously collected offline dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{offline}}$. During online training, transitions $(s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1})$ collected from real-environment interactions are stored in a replay buffer $\mathcal{D}$, and TD (Temporal Difference) learning is used to update the Q-function $Q_\phi$ and the policy.

Two baseline Q-learning algorithms are implemented to validate QWM:

- EXPO: A method that pairs a supervised pretrained base policy $\pi_{\text{base}}$ with a lightweight editing policy $\pi_{\text{edit}}$ trained to maximize Q-values. By clipping the edit magnitude to $[-\beta, \beta]$, it achieves highly efficient learning without destroying the base policy. During action selection, it selects the action that maximizes Q-values on the fly (OTF) from multiple candidates.

- RLPD: A SAC-based algorithm combining a high UTD (Update-to-Data) ratio—the number of network updates performed per real environment step—with an ensemble of critic networks and LayerNorm. It stabilizes training dramatically by sampling equally (50/50) from offline and online buffers.

sections.heading: QWM: Tree search combining Q-functions and world models
sections.summary: QWM expands a shallow search tree using a world model and determines actions by aggregating intermediate and leaf node values. It introduces a hybrid node evaluation combining Q-function long-term return estimation with world model rollout predictions, keeping computation low through beam search pruning with the Q-function.
sections.details:
The QWM algorithm consists of three stages: tree construction, value aggregation, and search pruning via the Q-function.

### 4.1 Tree Search Construction with World Models
The current state $s_0$ serves as the root (depth 0). At each state node at depth $d$, $N$ candidate actions $\{a_d^n\}_{n=1}^N \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot|s_d)$ are sampled from the current policy. For each action node, the world model $M_\psi$ is queried $K$ times to obtain predicted future states $\{s_{d+1}^k\}_{k=1}^K$, forming state nodes at depth $d+1$. This is expanded recursively up to depth $D$. Keeping the search depth $D$ deliberately shallow (predominantly $D=2$ in experiments) is critical, as it prevents the world model's own prediction errors from compounding.

### 4.2 Node Value Aggregation
To evaluate the search tree, the method introduces two complementary estimators:
- State-action value estimator $V_Q$: Directly scores the action using the critic (Q-function) ($V_Q(s_d, a_d) = Q_\phi(s_d, a_d)$). This is immune to model prediction errors and has low variance, but relies entirely on the accuracy of the learned Q-function.
- State value estimator $V_r$: Uses the step reward predicted by the world model and the discounted value of the next state ($V_r(s_d, a_d) = r_\psi(s_d, a_d) + \lambda \mathbb{E}[V(s_{d+1})]$). This reflects actual rollout dynamics, but accumulates model errors as depth increases.

Combining these, intermediate node values are defined as $V(s_d, a_d) = \frac{1}{2}(V_Q + V_r)$ (more generally, a weighted average with weight $\alpha$). The final score $Q_{ts}(s_0, a_0^n)$ for root actions $a_0^n$ is computed similarly, and the action with the highest tree-search score is executed.

### 4.3 Search Pruning with the Q-Function
Because tree size explodes with depth, QWM incorporates beam search pruning using the Q-function as an evaluation metric. The number of paths expanded at each depth is capped at $J$, retaining only the top-$J$ sub-paths with the highest cumulative scores and pruning the rest.

### 4.4 Implementation Details
In the sparse-reward environments evaluated in this work (where rewards are given only upon task completion), reward modeling in the world model is omitted, using only the transition dynamics model. For low-dimensional state observations, a 3-layer MLP (hidden dimension 256) residual dynamics model is used. For image (pixel) observations, a video world model based on the diffusion transformer video model 'Wan2.2-TI2V-5B' is constructed and fine-tuned, tokenizing actions via an MLP and concatenating them with text condition tokens.

sections.heading: Unmatched sample efficiency on challenging manipulation benchmarks
sections.summary: Evaluated on Robomimic and LIBERO benchmarks, QWM outperformed state-of-the-art model-free methods (DSRL, IDQL, etc.) and model-based methods (TD-MPC2, EfficientZero V2). It also showed clear gains in image-input tasks, with detailed ablations on search depth and sampling stages validating the approach.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on challenging tasks using a 7-DoF robot arm (Lift, Can, Square, and Tool Hang in Robomimic, plus 5 tasks in LIBERO). All tasks used a sparse reward setting where reward is given only upon task completion.

### 5.1 Comparison with Modern Model-Free and Model-Based Baselines
Compared to model-free baselines (RLPD, DSRL, QSM, QAM, FQL, IDQL), QWM consistently achieved the highest success rates and fastest learning speeds (Figure F2). In particular, it substantially outperformed IDQL, which samples multiple actions and picks the best one using immediate Q-values, demonstrating the superiority of predictive lookahead with a world model.
The comparison with model-based methods (TD-MPC2, EfficientZero V2) was even more striking (Figure F3). Existing MBRL methods struggled even in dense-reward settings, and in sparse-reward settings, their success rates remained near 0% on all tasks except the simplest, Lift. In contrast, because QWM grounds its Q-function in real-world data while searching, it reached nearly 100% success on the highly challenging Tool Hang task (a multi-stage tool assembly and hanging task) in around 200k steps.

### 5.2 Additive Gains on Base Algorithms
QWM was tested on top of both EXPO and RLPD. Compared to standalone EXPO (Figure F4) and standalone RLPD (Figure F5), adding tree search via QWM dramatically accelerated the onset of learning across all tasks. Combining QWM with EXPO, which already has high base performance, yielded the highest efficiency overall.

### 5.3 Scaling to Pixel Observations (Image Inputs)
Even on LIBERO tasks with pixel observations (Figure F6), where tree search was applied only during online data collection due to computational constraints, QWM consistently outperformed EXPO. This demonstrates that short-horizon lookahead with video world models remains effective in high-dimensional visual environments.

### 5.4 Ablation Analysis: What Drives Performance?
Key design components were thoroughly analyzed (Figure F7):
- Collection vs. Evaluation: Comparing search during data collection only (sample only), evaluation only (eval only), and both (sample + eval) revealed that using search in both stages performed best. A clear synergy emerged: collection search supplies high-quality data to the replay buffer, while evaluation search directly sharpens policy execution.
- Search Depth $D$: A depth of $D=2$ delivered the most consistent, high performance. $D=1$ provided insufficient future context, while deeper searches allowed world model errors to creep in.
- Discount Factor $\lambda$ and Candidate Count $N$: A moderate discount factor of around $\lambda=0.2$ worked best; larger values made the search sensitive to deep model errors. An action candidate count of around $N=8$ was optimal, as higher counts increased computational cost and noise susceptibility.
- Pruned Paths $J$: The number of retained paths $J$ after pruning proved robust; even with small values, the top promising branches were captured without performance loss.

sections.heading: Summary and open challenges: Compute overhead and high-fidelity models
sections.summary: QWM provides a framework to dramatically enhance Q-learning by confining world models to test-time tree search, sidestepping compounding model bias. However, practical constraints such as search compute overhead at each step and the training cost of high-quality world models remain, outlining directions for future work.
sections.details:
This paper introduced QWM, a framework that leverages the predictive capacity of world models for tree search during inference and data collection in Q-learning. Rather than training policies directly inside a world model, QWM grounds learning in real-world data, neatly resolving the issue of model prediction bias spiraling out of control in the training loop.

At the same time, the authors candidly discuss practical limitations:
- Inference Latency: Compared to standard policies requiring only a single forward pass, repeatedly querying the world model for tree search incurs non-negligible computational overhead. For real robots requiring high control frequencies, inference latency could become a bottleneck.
- World Model Training Cost: Pretraining high-fidelity world models, especially video diffusion models for pixel observations, demands substantial offline data and compute resources.

The authors conclude that accelerating search algorithms and constructing more lightweight, high-performance world models represent vital avenues for future research.

sections.heading: Appendix: Why search with action-value $Q$ instead of state-value $V$?
sections.summary: A direct comparison was conducted between searching solely with a state-value function $V$ (common in model-based RL) and searching with an action-value function $Q$ as in QWM. Whether applied to EXPO or standalone policies, searching with a $Q$-function proved overwhelmingly superior.
sections.details:
Many model-based RL methods use a state-value function $V(s)$ to evaluate terminal states during tree search or planning. To answer why QWM searches with a Q-function, the appendix investigates a comparison by training only a $V$-function and updating the policy via Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) during search.

Whether modifying EXPO's editing policy to be $V$-based (Figure F8) or modifying RLPD's Gaussian policy to be $V$-based, the results were unmistakable: searching with a $Q$-function dramatically outperformed searching with a $V$-function across all tasks.

The authors attribute this to two factors. First, $Q(s, a)$ provides estimates conditioned directly on actions, feeding a much higher-resolution signal into the search tree than $V(s)$. Second, the learning capacity of the underlying off-policy Q-learning algorithm is inherently stronger than $V$-based policy optimization. These findings strongly validate, both theoretically and empirically, that Q-learning is uniquely suited for integration with world models.

captions.F8: Comparison between searching with state-value $V$ versus action-value $Q$ (QWM-EXPO). Across all tasks, QWM incorporating the $Q$-function achieves overwhelmingly higher success rates.

takeaways: Using a world model as an action search tool during test-time and data collection is far more stable than using it to synthesize training data, as it prevents compounding model bias.
Keeping the search tree deliberately shallow ($D=2$) and delegating long-term return estimation to a critic (Q-function) is highly effective at containing model errors.
Applying test-time search during both data collection and evaluation creates a synergy between higher-quality replay buffer data and more precise action selection.
Using an action-conditioned $Q$-function as the search evaluation metric provides vastly higher search accuracy than relying on the traditional state-value function $V$.
limitations: Repeated policy sampling and world model rollouts during inference introduce significant computational overhead and latency compared to standard single-pass policies.
Pretraining video-generation-based world models, especially for pixel observations, remains computationally expensive and data-intensive.
Step-reward model learning was omitted because the focus was on sparse-reward tasks; scalability to complex dense-reward environments warrants further investigation.
